title: Choose what goes into a commit

scenario.brief:
**Where you are.** You edited two files this morning. `recipe.md` has a finished fix (a missing ingredient). `notes.md` has half-written thoughts you are not ready to save.

**The idea.** The staging area lets you save one change without the other. You add only the file you want; the other stays edited on disk but out of the commit.

**What you'll do.**

1. Run `git status`. Both files show as modified.
2. Run `git diff recipe.md` to see the fix, and `git diff notes.md` to see the half-done thoughts.
3. Stage only the recipe: `git add recipe.md`.
4. Commit: `git commit -m "Add missing salt to pancake recipe"`.
5. Run `git status` again. notes.md is still modified and unsaved. That is exactly right.

**Good to know.** Later you will learn `git add -p`, which lets you pick single lines from inside one file. For now, picking whole files is enough.
scenario.whyItMatters: Teammates review commits one at a time. A commit that mixes a finished fix with half-done notes is hard to review and impossible to reuse. Choosing what goes in is a daily skill.

objectives.title: Commit the recipe fix on its own
objectives.description: The newest commit must change only recipe.md.
hints: Add only the file you want saved. Do not use `git add .` here; it would grab both.
`git add recipe.md` stages just that file. `git status` shows recipe.md in green and notes.md still in red.
Type: `git add recipe.md` then `git commit -m "Add missing salt to pancake recipe"`

objectives.title: Leave the notes change unsaved
objectives.description: notes.md should still show as modified after your commit.
hints: Nothing to do if you only added recipe.md. Check with `git status`.
If you staged notes.md by accident, take it out of the box with `git restore --staged notes.md`. The edit stays in the file.
If you committed both files together, undo the commit but keep the edits: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, then `git restore --staged notes.md`, then commit recipe.md alone.

debrief.summary: You saved one change and deliberately left another unsaved. The staging area is what makes that possible.
internals: Both files were modified on disk. `git add recipe.md` copied only the recipe into the staging area.
`git commit` built a snapshot from the staging area, so notes.md in that snapshot is still the old version.
Your edited notes.md still sits on disk, unstaged. Git knows it changed (status shows it) but has not saved it.

keyCommands.note: Stage one file at a time.
See the changes in just one file.
Take a file back out of the staging area.

commonMistakes: Using `git add .` or `git commit -a` out of habit and sweeping unfinished work into the commit.
Panicking after committing too much. `git reset --soft HEAD~1` undoes the commit and keeps your work.
debrief.atWork: Reviewers love commits that do one thing. This habit is also what lets you cherry-pick a single fix onto a release later.
debrief.interview: "Why does Git have a staging area?" Answer: so you can shape each commit, saving some changes now and others later.

solution: git commit -m "Add missing salt to pancake recipe"
